input: "Tell her something you noticed because you wished she were here to notice it too. It can be small. You don't have to make the Academy sound impressive." I keep my eyes on my own page. "That would make me believe it, anyway." I leave him to write and work on my short story for the rest of the hour. If Ashara comes in, I make room and offer tea without asking her to account for the challenge at the door.
output:
Rashid’s pen hovers over the page for so long that the kettle cools between pours. Then he says, without looking up, “The bridge lamps are blue at dawn. She would like that.”

He writes it down.

A few lines later, he adds, “She would ask whether the food is edible.”

“That is a better question than whether the library has forbidden books,” Thessaly says, pressing soil around the rosemary’s roots.

Rashid’s mouth twitches. “I’ll tell her both.”

The hour acquires its own quiet shape. Seraphel finishes with the troublesome feather and folds her wing with a relieved little shiver; Thessaly carries the potted rosemary toward the garden light. Your own draft becomes a gathering of crossed-out beginnings and one paragraph you do not yet dislike. Across from you, Rashid eventually folds the letter without sealing it.

“Thank you,” he says, low enough not to make the room attend.

The hall door opens before you can answer. Ashara stands there in a dark training tunic, formal coat slung over one shoulder. Dust dulls the toes of her boots; one knuckle bears a fresh split, and a singed thread hangs from her cuff. Her hair is still tied severely, though several strands have escaped around one horn.

Her gaze takes in Rashid, the letter, Seraphel’s towel, Thessaly’s potting soil, and you.

“This is a remarkably populated version of no audience,” she says.

No one rises to demand an account. You draw an empty chair nearer the hearth and pour tea into a clean cup, leaving it waiting.

Ashara looks at the cup, then at you. Some of the tightness leaves her tail.

She takes the chair. “No honey.”

Rashid lowers his eyes to his folded letter. Seraphel becomes intensely occupied with the salve tin.

Ashara takes one careful drink. “I lost by one point,” she says. “If anyone calls it a useful lesson, I will throw them through a window.”
